citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
First fix a deterministic complex symmetric matrix $A$. Since $A_{ji}=A_{ij}$,
$$\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A
=\sum_i A_{ii}(\xi_i^2-1)+2\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}\xi_i\xi_j.$$
The diagonal summands have mean zero. Distinct diagonal summands are uncorrelated; a diagonal summand and an off-diagonal summand are uncorrelated because at least one independent centered coordinate occurs to the first power; and two off-diagonal summands are uncorrelated unless their unordered index pairs coincide. Therefore
$$\mathbb E\left|\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^2
=(\mu_4-1)\sum_i|A_{ii}|^2+4\sum_{i<j}|A_{ij}|^2
\le C_{\mu_4}\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|^2.$$
Here $\mu_4\ge1$ follows from $\mathbb E\xi_i^2=1$ and Cauchy–Schwarz.

By [F2], the joint law of $(\xi,A)$ is the product of its marginal laws. The integrand is integrable: $|\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A|^2\le2\|A\|_F^2\|\xi\|_2^4+2d\|A\|_F^2$, and $\mathbb E\|\xi\|_2^4<\infty$ because $d$ is finite and $\mathbb E\xi_i^4<\infty$. Thus [F3] permits integration of the deterministic inequality in step 1.1 against the law of $A$, giving the asserted bound.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

derivations.claim:
By [F1], write $B=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)U^{\mathsf T}$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$. Thus $R$ exists, is normal, and
$$x^{\mathsf T}Rx=\sum_j\frac{(U^{\mathsf T}x)_j^2}{\lambda_j-z},\qquad
\operatorname{Im}(x^{\mathsf T}Rx)=\eta\sum_j\frac{(U^{\mathsf T}x)_j^2}{(\lambda_j-u)^2+\eta^2}.$$
If $x\ne0$, this imaginary part is strictly positive, so $1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx\ne0$; if $x=0$, the denominator is $1$.

Direct multiplication verifies
$$(B+xx^{\mathsf T}-zI)\left(R-\frac{Rxx^{\mathsf T}R}{1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx}\right)=I.$$
Since $B+xx^{\mathsf T}$ is also real symmetric and $z\notin\mathbb R$, its resolvent exists; hence the displayed expression is $R_x$.

Taking traces in step 1.2 gives
$$\operatorname{tr}(R_x-R)=-\frac{x^{\mathsf T}R^2x}{1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx}.$$
In the eigenbasis of [F1],
$$|x^{\mathsf T}R^2x|\le\sum_j\frac{(U^{\mathsf T}x)_j^2}{(\lambda_j-u)^2+\eta^2}
=\frac{\operatorname{Im}(x^{\mathsf T}Rx)}{\eta}.$$
Also $|1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx|\ge\operatorname{Im}(x^{\mathsf T}Rx)$ when $x\ne0$; for $x=0$ the trace difference is zero. Combining these inequalities proves the stated $1/\eta$ bound.

For positive integers $n$ and $p$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and define its (uncentered, unit-variance-normalized) sample covariance matrix by
$$S(X):=\frac1nX^{\mathsf T}X\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}.$$
It is real symmetric and non-negative. If its eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are $\lambda_1(S(X)),\ldots,\lambda_p(S(X))$, its empirical spectral distribution (ESD), normalized by the matrix dimension $p$, is
$$\mu_{S(X)}:=\frac1p\sum_{j=1}^p\delta_{\lambda_j(S(X))}.$$
The largest eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\max}(S(X)):=\max_j\lambda_j(S(X))$. When $S(X)$ has at least one positive eigenvalue, its smallest positive eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S(X)):=\min\{\lambda_j(S(X)):\lambda_j(S(X))>0\}$. For a sequence $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$, write $S_n=S(X_n)$ and $\mu_n=\mu_{S_n}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $n\ge1$, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$. Define

$$P_n(A):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}(A),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$

Then $P_n$ is a probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

derivations.claim:
The matrix $S(X)$ is symmetric because $(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{\mathsf T}=X^{\mathsf T}X$. For every $v\in\mathbb R^p$,
$$v^{\mathsf T}S(X)v=\frac1n\|Xv\|_2^2\ge0.$$
By [F2], its eigenvalues are real; if $S(X)v=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, the displayed quadratic-form identity gives $\lambda\|v\|_2^2\ge0$, hence $\lambda\ge0$.

Apply [F3] to the finite list $\lambda_1(S(X)),\ldots,\lambda_p(S(X))$ in the Borel space $\mathbb R$. The resulting empirical measure is exactly [F1] and is a Borel probability measure. Step 1.1 shows it assigns no mass outside $[0,\infty)$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $B$ be a real symmetric non-negative $d\times d$ matrix, let $x\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$. Put $R=(B-zI)^{-1}$ and $R_x=(B+xx^{\mathsf T}-zI)^{-1}$. Then $1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx\ne0$,
$$R_x=R-\frac{Rxx^{\mathsf T}R}{1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx},$$
and
$$\left|\operatorname{tr}R_x-\operatorname{tr}R\right|\le\frac1\eta.$$

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward ([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). Put $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$ on the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be product-measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic constants $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(z_1,\ldots,z_i,\ldots,z_n)-f(z_1,\ldots,z_i',\ldots,z_n)|\le c_i$$
for every fixed setting of the other coordinates and every $z_i,z_i'$. The independent product-law theorem identifies the law of $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ as $\mu$. Applying change of variables for expectation first to $|f|$ and then to $f$ makes $f(Z)$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E f(Z)=\int f\,d\mu$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2$. For $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\bigl(f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)-\mathbb E f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ this probability is $0$. The same bound holds for the lower tail, so the two-sided probability is at most $2e^{-2t^2/V}$ when $V>0$.

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

derivations.claim: Fix all vectors except $Y_{n,j}$. Replacing that vector by another vector $Y'_{n,j}$ changes $B_n$ by removing $Y_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^{\mathsf T}$ and adding $Y'_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^{\mathsf T}$. Applying [F1] once to remove the first term and once to add the second shows that $\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}$ changes by at most $2/\eta$. Hence each of the real and imaginary parts of $M_n(z)$ has coordinate oscillation at most $c_j=2/(d_n\eta)$.

Apply [F2] separately to $\operatorname{Re}M_n(z)$ and $\operatorname{Im}M_n(z)$. If a complex number has modulus greater than $t$, at least one of its real or imaginary parts has magnitude greater than $t/\sqrt2$. The union bound therefore gives
$$\Pr\{|M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)|>t\}
\le4\exp\left(-\frac{t^2d_n^2\eta^2}{4N_n}\right).$$
This is the stated estimate.
Since $d_n/n\to c>0$, for each fixed $t>0$ the exponent in step 1.2 is at most $-c_tn$ for all sufficiently large $n$, for some $c_t>0$. The probabilities are therefore summable.
Apply [F3] to the events in step 2.1 for each $t=1/k$, $k\ge1$, and intersect the resulting countable collection of probability-one events. On that event $M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)\to0$.

For $\gamma>0$, set
$$a_\gamma=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad r_+:=\max\{r,0\}\quad(r\in\mathbb R).$$
Define the Marchenko–Pastur set function on Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ by
$$\mu_\gamma(A):=\int_{A\cap(a_\gamma,b_\gamma)}\frac{\sqrt{(b_\gamma-x)(x-a_\gamma)}}{2\pi\gamma x}\,d\lambda(x)+\left(1-\frac1\gamma\right)_+\delta_0(A),$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. The formula defines a finite Borel measure; its total mass is established by the Marchenko–Pastur law below.

If two holomorphic functions on a complex domain agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain, then they agree everywhere on the domain.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain ([[def-complex-domain]]), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim:
Put $B=2\sqrt\gamma$, $A_0=1+\gamma$, and $x(\theta)=A_0+B\cos\theta$ for $0<\theta<\pi$. This substitution maps $(0,\pi)$ onto $(a,b)$ in reverse order, with $\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}=B\sin\theta$ and $|dx|=B\sin\theta\,d\theta$. Thus the continuous part of $\mu_\gamma$ becomes $(2/\pi)\sin^2\theta\,d\theta/x(\theta)$. For real $A>B$, the substitution $t=\tan(\theta/2)$ gives
$$\int_0^\pi\frac{d\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}=2\int_0^\infty\frac{dt}{(A+B)+(A-B)t^2}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{A^2-B^2}}.$$
Write $I_0(A)=\int_0^\pi(A+B\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\pi/\sqrt{A^2-B^2}$. Since $\int_0^\pi\cos\theta\,d\theta=0$ and $\cos\theta/(A+B\cos\theta)=B^{-1}-A/[B(A+B\cos\theta)]$,
$$I_1(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\cos\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}d\theta=\frac\pi B-\frac A B I_0(A),\quad I_2(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\cos^2\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}d\theta=-\frac A B I_1(A)=-\frac{A\pi}{B^2}+\frac{A^2}{B^2}I_0(A).$$
Therefore
$$J(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin^2\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}\,d\theta=I_0(A)-I_2(A)=\frac{\pi(A-\sqrt{A^2-B^2})}{B^2}.$$
For $A=A_0>B$, the root is $|1-\gamma|$; if $\gamma=1$, direct cancellation $\sin^2\theta/(2+2\cos\theta)= (1-\cos\theta)/2$ gives the same value by continuity. Hence the continuous mass is $2J(A_0)/\pi=(A_0-|1-\gamma|)/(2\gamma)=\min(1,\gamma)/\gamma$. Adding $(1-1/\gamma)_+$ gives total mass one; the density is nonnegative and integrable by this finite integral, and its support is nonnegative.

For $w=re^{i\theta}\in\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$, with $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta<\pi$, define $q_0(w)=\sqrt r\,e^{i\theta/2}$. This is continuous, satisfies $q_0(w)^2=w$, and is holomorphic: for $h\to0$ with $w+h$ in the slit plane,
$$\frac{q_0(w+h)-q_0(w)}h=\frac1{q_0(w+h)+q_0(w)}\longrightarrow\frac1{2q_0(w)}.$$
Set $\Omega=\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,B]$ and $q(A)=q_0(A-B)q_0(A+B)$ for $A\in\Omega$. Both factors are defined and holomorphic there, $q(A)^2=A^2-B^2$, and $q(A)>0$ for real $A>B$. The domain is connected: each $A-B=re^{i\theta}$ with $-\pi<\theta<\pi$ can be joined inside it to $B+1$ by continuously changing $r$ to $1$ and $\theta$ to $0$. The integral $J(A)$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$. Indeed, on any compact subset its denominator is bounded away from zero, and the difference quotient of its integrand tends pointwise to $-\sin^2\theta/(A+B\cos\theta)^2$ with a uniform integrable bound; [F3] justifies passing that limit through the integral. The identity theorem [F2] extends the formula from real $A>B$ (which has limit points inside $\Omega$) to all $A\in\Omega$. In particular it applies to $A_z=A_0-z$, whose imaginary part is negative.

Let $q=\sqrt{(1+\gamma-z)^2-4\gamma}$ on that branch. The substitution in step 1.1 and $1/[x(x-z)]=z^{-1}((x-z)^{-1}-x^{-1})$ give the transform of the continuous part as $[(A_z-q)-(A_0-|1-\gamma|)]/(2\gamma z)$. Adding the atom contributes $-(1-1/\gamma)_+/z$; simplifying in the cases $\gamma\le1$ and $\gamma>1$ gives
$$m_\gamma(z)=\frac{1-\gamma-z-q}{2\gamma z}.$$
Since $q^2=(1-\gamma-z)^2-4\gamma z$, substitution verifies $\gamma z m_\gamma(z)^2+(z+\gamma-1)m_\gamma(z)+1=0$, which is the fixed-point equation in the Statement.

For $x\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}(z/(x-z))=\eta x/|x-z|^2\ge0$. Integrating this identity against the probability measure from step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{Im}(z m_\gamma(z))\ge0$, so $\operatorname{Im}(1-\gamma-z-\gamma z m_\gamma(z))=-\eta-\gamma\operatorname{Im}(z m_\gamma(z))\le-\eta$.

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$. For $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, its Stieltjes transform, with the $(x-z)^{-1}$ convention, is
$$m_\mu(z):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{x-z}\,d\mu(x).$$
The integral is finite because $|x-z|^{-1}\le\eta^{-1}$ for every real $x$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim:
For $\eta>0$, the imaginary part of the integrand in [F1] is $\eta/((x-u)^2+\eta^2)$. Fubini [F2] therefore gives
$$\frac1\pi\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(u+i\eta)\,du=\int K_{\eta,a,b}(x)\,d\mu(x),\quad K_{\eta,a,b}(x)=\frac1\pi\left(\arctan\frac{b-x}{\eta}-\arctan\frac{a-x}{\eta}\right).$$
The kernel lies in $[0,1]$ and tends pointwise to $1$ on $(a,b)$, $1/2$ at either endpoint, and $0$ elsewhere. [F3] gives the interval formula in the Statement, including endpoint atoms.

For any $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$\eta\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(x+i\eta)=\int\frac{\eta^2}{(t-x)^2+\eta^2}\,d\mu(t).$$
The integrand is bounded by $1$ and tends to $\mathbf1_{\{x\}}(t)$ as $\eta\downarrow0$. Dominated convergence [F3] proves the atom formula.
If $m_\mu=m_\nu$, step 1.2 gives equality of their point masses at every $x$. Step 1.1 then gives $\mu((a,b))=\nu((a,b))$ for every $a<b$.

The family $\mathcal P=\{\varnothing,\mathbb R\}\cup\{(a,b):a<b\}$ is a pi-system: the intersection of two open intervals is another open interval or empty. It generates the Borel sigma-algebra because open intervals form a basis. The class of Borel sets on which $\mu$ and $\nu$ agree is a lambda-system: it contains $\mathbb R$ because both measures are probabilities, is closed under complements by finite total mass, and is closed under disjoint countable unions by countable additivity. Step 2.1 and [F4] therefore give equality on every Borel set, so $\mu=\nu$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For positive integers $n$ and $p$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and define its (uncentered, unit-variance-normalized) sample covariance matrix by
$$S(X):=\frac1nX^{\mathsf T}X\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}.$$
It is real symmetric and non-negative. If its eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are $\lambda_1(S(X)),\ldots,\lambda_p(S(X))$, its empirical spectral distribution (ESD), normalized by the matrix dimension $p$, is
$$\mu_{S(X)}:=\frac1p\sum_{j=1}^p\delta_{\lambda_j(S(X))}.$$
The largest eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\max}(S(X)):=\max_j\lambda_j(S(X))$. When $S(X)$ has at least one positive eigenvalue, its smallest positive eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S(X)):=\min\{\lambda_j(S(X)):\lambda_j(S(X))>0\}$. For a sequence $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$, write $S_n=S(X_n)$ and $\mu_n=\mu_{S_n}$.

For positive integers $n,p$ and a real matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, set $S(X)=X^{\mathsf T}X/n$ and $\mu_{S(X)}=p^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^p\delta_{\lambda_j(S(X))}$, where the eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity. Then $\mu_{S(X)}$ is a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$, supported on $[0,\infty)$.

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$. For $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, its Stieltjes transform, with the $(x-z)^{-1}$ convention, is
$$m_\mu(z):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{x-z}\,d\mu(x).$$
The integral is finite because $|x-z|^{-1}\le\eta^{-1}$ for every real $x$.

Let $\xi=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d)^{\mathsf T}$ have independent identically distributed real coordinates with $\mathbb E\xi_i=0$, $\mathbb E\xi_i^2=1$, and $\mu_4:=\mathbb E\xi_i^4<\infty$. Let $A$ be an independent random complex symmetric $d\times d$ matrix with $\mathbb E\|A\|_F^2<\infty$, where $\|A\|_F^2:=\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|^2$. Then
$$\mathbb E\left|\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^2\le C_{\mu_4}\,\mathbb E\|A\|_F^2,\qquad C_{\mu_4}:=\max\{\mu_4-1,2\}.$$

Let $B$ be a real symmetric non-negative $d\times d$ matrix, let $x\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$. Put $R=(B-zI)^{-1}$ and $R_x=(B+xx^{\mathsf T}-zI)^{-1}$. Then $1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx\ne0$,
$$R_x=R-\frac{Rxx^{\mathsf T}R}{1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx},$$
and
$$\left|\operatorname{tr}R_x-\operatorname{tr}R\right|\le\frac1\eta.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For each positive integer $n$, let $Y_{n,1},\ldots,Y_{n,n}$ be independent random vectors in $\mathbb R^{d_n}$, let $B_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n}Y_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^{\mathsf T}$, and let $z=u+i\eta$ with fixed $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$. Define
$$M_n(z):=\frac1{d_n}\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}.$$
If $d_n/n\to c$ for some $c\in(0,\infty)$, then $M_n(z)-\mathbb E[M_n(z)]\to0$ almost surely. More precisely, for every $t>0$,
$$\Pr\left\{|M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)|>t\right\}
\le4\exp\left(-\frac{t^2d_n^2\eta^2}{4n}\right).$$

For every $\gamma>0$, the set function $\mu_\gamma$ in the definition of the Marchenko–Pastur measure is a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$. For every $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\eta:=\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its Stieltjes transform $m_\gamma(z)$ satisfies
$$1+z m_\gamma(z)=\frac{m_\gamma(z)}{1+\gamma m_\gamma(z)},\qquad \operatorname{Im}\bigl(1-\gamma-z-\gamma z m_\gamma(z)\bigr)\le-\eta.$$

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$, with Stieltjes transform $m_\mu(z)=\int (x-z)^{-1}\,d\mu(x)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. For every $a<b$ and $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$\mu((a,b))+\tfrac12\mu(\{a\})+\tfrac12\mu(\{b\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\frac1\pi\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(u+i\eta)\,du,\qquad \mu(\{x\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\eta\,\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(x+i\eta).$$
If two Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R$ have the same Stieltjes transform on the upper half-plane, then they are equal.
Assume AC. A tight sequence of Borel probability laws on a Polish S has a subsequence converging weakly to a Borel probability on that same S.

For every finite real random variable $X$ and every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge t)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{t^2}.$$
Equivalently, if $\sigma_X>0$ and $c>0$, then $\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge c\sigma_X)\le1/c^2$. If $\sigma_X=0$, the first form remains valid for every $t>0$.

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_n)$ and $X$ be real random variables on one probability space.  Write
$X_n\to X$ **almost surely** when
$$\mathbb P\bigl(\{\omega:X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\text{ in }\mathbb R\}\bigr)=1.$$
The convergence in the event is the real convergence of [[def-real-limit]].
The set is measurable by [[lem-almost-sure-convergence-event-is-measurable]],
so its probability is defined.

derivations.claim:
Fix $z=u+i\eta$ with $\eta>0$. Write the transpose of row $i$ of $X_n$ as $y_i\in\mathbb R^{p_n}$ and set $Q=(S_n-zI)^{-1}$, $m_n=p_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}Q=m_{\mu_n}(z)$ by [F1] and [F2]. For each $i$, let $S_i=S_n-y_iy_i^{\mathsf T}/n$, $Q_i=(S_i-zI)^{-1}$ and $\beta_i=n^{-1}y_i^{\mathsf T}Q_i y_i$. The matrices $S_n,S_i$ are nonnegative symmetric, so their resolvents exist; diagonalizing $S_i$ shows $\operatorname{Im}\beta_i\ge0$ and hence $1+\beta_i\ne0$. Applying [F4] with $x=y_i/\sqrt n$ gives $Q=Q_i-Q_i y_i y_i^{\mathsf T}Q_i/[n(1+\beta_i)]$, so $n^{-1}y_i^{\mathsf T}Qy_i=\beta_i/(1+\beta_i)$. Since $S_nQ=I+zQ$, taking normalized traces yields
$$1+z m_n=\frac1{p_n}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\beta_i}{1+\beta_i}.$$

Put $\gamma_n=p_n/n$, $v_n=\gamma_n m_n=n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}Q$, and $\mu_4=\mathbb E\xi^4$ for the common entry law. Both $\beta_i$ and $v_n$ have nonnegative imaginary part. Conditional on $Q_i$, row $y_i$ is independent of it by [F12]. Applying [F3] conditionally and using $\|Q_i\|_F^2\le p_n/\eta^2$ gives
$$\mathbb E\left|\beta_i-\frac1n\operatorname{tr}Q_i\right|\le\frac{\sqrt{C p_n}}{n\eta},\qquad C=\max\{\mu_4-1,2\}.$$
By [F4], $|\operatorname{tr}Q_i-\operatorname{tr}Q|\le1/\eta$, hence $\mathbb E|\beta_i-v_n|\le(\sqrt{Cp_n}+1)/(n\eta)$. For $f(w)=w/(1+w)$ and $\operatorname{Im}w,\operatorname{Im}v\ge0$, $|f(w)-f(v)|=|w-v|/(|1+w||1+v|)\le|w-v|$. Therefore [step 1.1] implies
$$\mathbb E\left|1+zm_n-\frac{m_n}{1+\gamma_n m_n}\right|\le\frac{\sqrt{Cp_n}+1}{p_n\eta}\longrightarrow0.$$

Apply [F5] to the independent vectors $y_i/\sqrt n$, whose rank-one sum is $S_n$. For the fixed $z$, $m_n-a_n\to0$ almost surely, where $a_n=\mathbb E m_n$. Also $\mathbb E|m_n-a_n|\to0$: for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\mathbb E|m_n-a_n|\le\varepsilon+(2/\eta)\Pr(|m_n-a_n|>\varepsilon)$, and the tail bound in [F5] makes the second term tend to zero. Define $g_n(w)=1+zw-w/(1+\gamma_nw)$. If $\operatorname{Im}w,\operatorname{Im}v\ge0$, then $|g_n(w)-g_n(v)|\le(|z|+1)|w-v|$. Taking expectations in the estimate of step 1.2 gives $g_n(a_n)\to0$.

The sequence $(a_n)$ is bounded by $1/\eta$. Moreover $\operatorname{Im}(z m_n)=p_n^{-1}\sum_j\eta\lambda_j(S_n)/|\lambda_j(S_n)-z|^2\ge0$, so $\operatorname{Im}(1-\gamma_n-z-\gamma_n z a_n)\le-\eta$. Every convergent subsequence of $a_n$ therefore has a limit $a$ satisfying $1+za=a/(1+\gamma a)$ and $\operatorname{Im}(1-\gamma-z-\gamma za)\le-\eta$. The two roots of the associated quadratic have corresponding values $D_j=1-\gamma-z-\gamma z a_j$ whose sum is $1-\gamma-z$, with imaginary part $-\eta$. Thus at most one root can have $\operatorname{Im}D_j\le-\eta$. By [F6], that root is $m_\gamma(z)$. All subsequential limits are consequently $m_\gamma(z)$, so $a_n\to m_\gamma(z)$ and step 2.1 gives $m_n(z)\to m_\gamma(z)$ almost surely.

Perform steps 1.1–2.2 for each $z$ in the countable dense set $\{u+i\eta:u,\eta\in\mathbb Q,\eta>0\}$ and intersect their probability-one events. Also let $T_n=(np_n)^{-1}\sum_{i,j}X_{n,ij}^2$. Its mean is one and its variance is $(\mu_4-1)/(np_n)$. Since $p_n/n\to\gamma>0$, [F9] gives a summable bound $\Pr(|T_n-1|>\varepsilon)\le(\mu_4-1)/(\varepsilon^2np_n)$ for every $\varepsilon>0$; [F10] over positive rational $\varepsilon$ yields $T_n\to1$ almost surely.

On this probability-one event, $\int x\,d\mu_n(x)=T_n$ and $\mu_n$ is supported on $[0,\infty)$ by [F1]. For every $R>0$, $\mu_n((R,\infty))\le T_n/R$, so the sequence is tight. By [A1] and [F8], every subsequence has a further weakly convergent subsequence with limit $
u$. Along it, [F11] applied to $x\mapsto(x-z)^{-1}$ shows $m_
u(z)=m_\gamma(z)$ on the dense set from step 3.1. The transforms are continuous because $|m_
u(z)-m_
u(w)|\le|z-w|/(\operatorname{Im}z\operatorname{Im}w)$ for $z,w\in\mathbb C^+$; equality therefore extends to all $z\in\mathbb C^+$.

By [F7], every weak subsequential limit $\nu$ in step 3.2 equals $\mu_\gamma$. If $\mu_n$ did not converge weakly to $\mu_\gamma$, some bounded continuous test function and a subsequence would have integrals separated from its $\mu_\gamma$ integral by a fixed positive amount; tightness would give a further weakly convergent subsequence, contradicting its limit $\mu_\gamma$. Therefore $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu_\gamma$ almost surely.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $\gamma>0$, set
$$a_\gamma=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad r_+:=\max\{r,0\}\quad(r\in\mathbb R).$$
Define the Marchenko–Pastur set function on Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ by
$$\mu_\gamma(A):=\int_{A\cap(a_\gamma,b_\gamma)}\frac{\sqrt{(b_\gamma-x)(x-a_\gamma)}}{2\pi\gamma x}\,d\lambda(x)+\left(1-\frac1\gamma\right)_+\delta_0(A),$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. The formula defines a finite Borel measure; its total mass is established by the Marchenko–Pastur law below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For each positive integer $n$, let $p_n$ be a positive integer with $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$, and let $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$ have mutually independent entries with one common law, mean zero, variance one, and finite fourth moment. Set $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and let $\mu_n$ be its empirical spectral distribution normalized by $p_n$. Then $\mu_n$ converges weakly almost surely to the probability measure with density
$$\rho_\gamma(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sqrt{(b_\gamma-x)(x-a_\gamma)}}{2\pi\gamma x},&a_\gamma<x<b_\gamma,\\0,&x\notin(a_\gamma,b_\gamma),\end{cases}\qquad a_\gamma=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\quad b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2,$$
and an atom of mass $(1-1/\gamma)_+$ at zero.

For each positive integer $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$ have mutually independent entries with one common law of mean zero, variance one, and finite fourth moment, and suppose $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. For $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$, the largest eigenvalue satisfies
$$\lambda_{\max}(S_n)\longrightarrow(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For each positive integer $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$ have mutually independent entries with one common law of mean zero, variance one, and finite fourth moment, and suppose $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. Set $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and let $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)$ denote its smallest positive eigenvalue whenever one exists. If $\gamma<1$, then almost surely $X_n$ has full column rank for all sufficiently large $n$, so $S_n$ has no zero eigenvalues eventually and $\lambda_{\min}(S_n)\to(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$. If $\gamma>1$, then almost surely $X_n$ has full row rank for all sufficiently large $n$, so $S_n$ has exactly $p_n-n$ zero eigenvalues and $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)\to(\sqrt\gamma-1)^2$. If $\gamma=1$, then almost surely $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)\to0$.

derivations.claim: Since $\sqrt\gamma=1/2$, the endpoints are $a=(1-1/2)^2=1/4$ and $b=(1+1/2)^2=9/4$, while the zero atom is $(1-4)_+=0$. Substituting in [F1] gives the displayed density on $(1/4,9/4)$ and zero outside.

The constants in [L2]–[L3] specialize to $b=9/4$ and $a=1/4$; [L1] specializes the limit law to the same density computed in step 1.1. These are conditional interface substitutions only: the local proofs of [L2] and [L3] remain unresolved, so this Example is escalated for its random-matrix conclusions.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $\gamma>0$, set
$$a_\gamma=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad r_+:=\max\{r,0\}\quad(r\in\mathbb R).$$
Define the Marchenko–Pastur set function on Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ by
$$\mu_\gamma(A):=\int_{A\cap(a_\gamma,b_\gamma)}\frac{\sqrt{(b_\gamma-x)(x-a_\gamma)}}{2\pi\gamma x}\,d\lambda(x)+\left(1-\frac1\gamma\right)_+\delta_0(A),$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. The formula defines a finite Borel measure; its total mass is established by the Marchenko–Pastur law below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For each positive integer $n$, let $p_n$ be a positive integer with $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$, and let $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$ have mutually independent entries with one common law, mean zero, variance one, and finite fourth moment. Set $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and let $\mu_n$ be its empirical spectral distribution normalized by $p_n$. Then $\mu_n$ converges weakly almost surely to the probability measure with density
$$\rho_\gamma(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sqrt{(b_\gamma-x)(x-a_\gamma)}}{2\pi\gamma x},&a_\gamma<x<b_\gamma,\\0,&x\notin(a_\gamma,b_\gamma),\end{cases}\qquad a_\gamma=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\quad b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2,$$
and an atom of mass $(1-1/\gamma)_+$ at zero.

For each positive integer $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$ have mutually independent entries with one common law of mean zero, variance one, and finite fourth moment, and suppose $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. For $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$, the largest eigenvalue satisfies
$$\lambda_{\max}(S_n)\longrightarrow(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For each positive integer $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$ have mutually independent entries with one common law of mean zero, variance one, and finite fourth moment, and suppose $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. Set $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and let $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)$ denote its smallest positive eigenvalue whenever one exists. If $\gamma<1$, then almost surely $X_n$ has full column rank for all sufficiently large $n$, so $S_n$ has no zero eigenvalues eventually and $\lambda_{\min}(S_n)\to(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$. If $\gamma>1$, then almost surely $X_n$ has full row rank for all sufficiently large $n$, so $S_n$ has exactly $p_n-n$ zero eigenvalues and $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)\to(\sqrt\gamma-1)^2$. If $\gamma=1$, then almost surely $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)\to0$.

derivations.claim: At $\gamma=1$, the endpoints are $a=0$ and $b=4$, and the atom is zero. On $(0,4)$ the density simplifies as $\sqrt{(4-x)x}/(2\pi x)=\sqrt{4-x}/(2\pi\sqrt{x})$, giving the formula in the Example.

The constants in [L2]–[L3] specialize to largest edge $4$ and smallest-positive edge $0$; [L1] specializes the limit law to the density computed in step 1.1. These are interface substitutions only; the edge proofs remain unresolved, so the Example is escalated for its random-matrix conclusions.
